In Indian sporting history, few careers carry an irony as striking as that of MJ Gopalan. A gifted cricketer and hockey player, Gopalan found himself facing an extraordinary choice in 1936: pursue a place in the Indian hockey team for the Berlin Olympics under legendary captain Dhyan Chand, or travel to England with the Indian cricket side. He chose cricket, following his greater passion. But what followed made the decision one of the most fascinating "what if" moments in Indian sport. The Indian hockey team went on to win Olympic gold in Berlin, while Gopalan, despite being part of the cricket tour he had chosen, did not get an opportunity to play a Test in England. Gopalan was a genuine double international, representing India in both cricket and hockey. Born in Morappakam and raised in Triplicane, Chennai, he emerged as a fast-medium bowler capable of moving the ball both ways and became one of the leading figures in Madras cricket. His cricketing talent was spotted by CP Johnstone, one of the founding figures of Madras cricket, and Gopalan soon made his mark in local cricket. His first-class career eventually brought him 194 wickets and 2,916 runs in 78 matches, making him far more successful at that level than his modest international record would suggest.

Cricket over Berlin Olympics with Dhyan Chand

Gopalan's hockey career was also significant. He played as a centre-half and, in 1935, toured New Zealand with the Indian hockey side, which enjoyed considerable success. That experience put him firmly in the reckoning for the 1936 Olympic squad. But when the opportunity came to compete for a place in the hockey team for the Berlin Games, Gopalan chose not to pursue the Olympic route. Instead, he accepted his place on the cricket tour of England. It was a decision that looked very different once the Berlin Olympics were over. India, led by Dhyan Chand, produced one of the most dominant campaigns in Olympic hockey history and won the gold medal after defeating Germany 8-1 in the final. Gopalan, who had been faced with the possibility of being part of that historic side, was instead in England with the cricket team. The irony became even greater because his opportunities on the cricket tour were limited. With Mohammad Nissar and Amar Singh ahead of him, Gopalan was not expected to play a major role, and he ultimately did not play a Test in England.

Gopalan had already made his Test debut before the 1936 tour, playing his only Test for India against England at Calcutta in the 1933-34 season. He took one wicket and scored 18 runs. Despite his reputation in domestic cricket, that remained his only appearance at Test level. His first-class record, however, reflected the quality of the cricketer he was. Gopalan took 194 wickets and scored 2,916 runs in 78 matches, while his batting improved significantly as his career progressed. He also captained Madras for several years and remained one of the most influential figures in the city's cricketing circles for around 25 years. But perhaps the most remarkable chapter of Gopalan's cricket career came not in Test cricket, but at the very beginning of India's premier domestic competition.

He bowled the first ball in Ranji Trophy history

When the Ranji Trophy was inaugurated in 1934, Madras and Mysore played the competition's first-ever match. Gopalan was given the honour of bowling the first delivery in Ranji Trophy history. That moment ensured that, regardless of the brevity of his Test career, his name would remain permanently linked to one of the most important competitions in Indian cricket. The Ranji Trophy would become the country's premier first-class tournament and a crucial pathway for generations of Indian cricketers. Gopalan's legacy in Madras cricket continued well beyond his playing career. He later served as a national selector in the 1950s and remained a respected figure in Indian cricket. In 1952, a silver jubilee fund was started to mark his 25 years in cricket and hockey, while the annual contest between Madras and Ceylon was named the MJ Gopalan Trophy. The competition continued for decades, underlining the esteem in which he was held.

Gopalan's connection with Chennai cricket was eventually honoured at the city's iconic MA Chidambaram Stadium. One of the entrances at the famous Chepauk stadium is named after him, ensuring that his name remains part of the physical landscape of Indian cricket. His career therefore presents a remarkable contradiction. He was good enough to represent India in two sports and was considered for an Olympic hockey team captained by Dhyan Chand, yet his cricket career at the highest international level consisted of only one Test. The England tour that he chose over the Berlin Olympics did not give him the opportunities he might have expected, while the hockey team he left behind returned from Germany as Olympic champions. Yet Gopalan's choice should not simply be viewed as a mistake. Cricket was his passion, and in 1936 he chose the sport he loved. What makes the decision so compelling is the benefit of hindsight. Had he pursued hockey and made the Olympic squad, he could have been part of Dhyan Chand's gold-medal-winning team and one of the most celebrated sporting groups in India's history. Instead, he became part of a different kind of history. He chose cricket over a chance at Olympic gold with Dhyan Chand, played only one Test for India, but bowled the first ball in Ranji Trophy history. His name lives on at Chepauk, his first-class record remains impressive, and his story continues to stand as one of Indian sport's great unanswered "what ifs". Gopalan died in December 2003 after a long life in Indian sport. At the time of his death, he was regarded as the oldest surviving Test cricketer.

articles.title: ‘I urge other cricketers to speak up’: Moin Khan makes emotional appeal for Imran Khan
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan wicketkeeper-batter Moin Khan has joined the growing chorus of voices expressing concern over the deteriorating health of f.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan wicketkeeper-batter Moin Khan has joined the growing chorus of voices expressing concern over the deteriorating health of former Pakistan captain and 1992 World Cup-winning leader Imran Khan, urging the country's authorities to ensure that the 73-year-old receives proper medical treatment in jail.Moin, a key member of Pakistan's World Cup-winning side under Imran, released an emotional video message on Saturday in which he appealed to the government, Adiala jail authorities and fellow cricketers to stand up for the former all-rounder. His intervention came shortly after batting great Javed Miandad also made an impassioned appeal in support of Imran.Imran has been incarcerated at Adiala jail in Rawalpindi since 2023 after being convicted in corruption cases, which he continues to deny. Concerns over his health have intensified in recent months, with reports of medical problems and allegations of inadequate medical care.‘His right to medical care should be honoured’Moin, who played alongside Imran during Pakistan's celebrated 1992 World Cup campaign, said the former captain's contribution to Pakistan cricket could not be forgotten and urged authorities to fulfil his right to receive medical treatment.“Our captain Imran Khan, as you all know, is currently in Adiala jail, and his condition is quite bad at present. One more time, I will urge the authorities, the government of Pakistan and all those people who run the Adiala jail,” Moin said in his video.“My request is that our captain’s right, as a former prime minister, as a citizen of Pakistan, his right to medical care should be honoured. Whatever he needs, it should be seen to,” he added.Moin then made a direct appeal to fellow cricketers to publicly support Imran.“Besides, I also urge other cricketers to speak up and voice their support for him. Imran Khan’s contribution to Pakistan cricket [is immense] and all of us who played in his era learnt a lot from him. He has given Pakistan cricket a lot,” he said.The plea comes amid increasing concern over Imran's health and follows a similar public appeal from Miandad. Pakistan's Supreme Court recently ordered that Imran be taken to hospital for medical examinations. He was subsequently taken to hospital before being returned to prison.Former cricketers rally behind ImranThe concerns have also prompted a group of former international captains to call for better medical care for Imran. 22 former captains from countries including India, England, the West Indies and New Zealand wrote to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif seeking adequate healthcare and constitutional safeguards for the former Pakistan captain. The letter followed an earlier appeal by 14 former captains in February.Australia captain Pat Cummins has also publicly backed the former captains' appeal.Australia great Greg Chappell, who played an important role in bringing former cricketers together in support of Imran, recently painted a worrying picture of his condition.“At the moment, he's not getting any better. You know, from a physical point of view, it's hard to get information, but I saw a video clip the other day, I'm assuming, of his latest trip to hospital where he was put into a wheelchair to get him to, from wherever he was, to wherever he was going, and he didn't look well at all. He didn't look robust. He didn't look like he could really... get around very much,” Chappell said.“I mean, 73 years of age, so obviously, you know, he's getting older, but, you know, I met up with him in Pakistan 6 years ago, and he was still a strong, robust older man. That's not the case anymore. His right eye apparently [has developed a disability]… he's struggling. He's been in isolation for 3 years,” he added.The issue has also spilled into the cricketing world. The Pakistan Cricket Board lodged a formal complaint against Sky Sports after an interview with Imran's sons, Suleiman and Kasim Khan, was aired during the lunch break on the first day of the ongoing Test at Lord's.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Off-field stuff, we don’t focus on it': Muzumdar refuses to be drawn into India-Pakistan handshake debate
articles.summary: Cricket News: India women's head coach Amol Muzumdar on Saturday refused to be drawn into questions over the handshake protocol ahead of the team's Women's Asia Cup.
articles.body: India women's head coach Amol Muzumdar on Saturday refused to be drawn into questions over the handshake protocol ahead of the team's Women's Asia Cup clash against Pakistan on September 5.With India set to face Pakistan again, Muzumdar said the team was focused solely on its opening game against Thailand on Sunday and would address the issue when the two sides meet.“We try to play the best cricket on the ground and off the field stuff, we don't focus on it. We try to play the best cricket that we know on that particular day. We will speak about this when we play that game. But at the moment, we are focusing on tomorrow's game. One game at a time,” Muzumdar said at the pre-match press conference.Handshake protocol continuesThe no-handshake stance between Indian and Pakistani cricket teams has been in place since the 2025 Men's Asia Cup, following the Pahalgam terror attack in April that year. India avoided handshakes with Pakistan in all three meetings during that tournament, including the final. The stance was subsequently maintained across senior, women's and age-group cricket.The Indian women's team followed the protocol during their Women's ODI World Cup meeting with Pakistan in Colombo in October 2025. It was also observed during the Men's Rising Stars Asia Cup, the Under-19 Asia Cup, the Under-19 World Cup and the Men's T20 World Cup.The stance continued during the Women's T20 World Cup clash between India and Pakistan in Birmingham in June 2026, when Harmanpreet Kaur's team again did not exchange handshakes with their opponents.India look to move on from poor T20I formMuzumdar also played down India's recent T20I record, with the team having lost nine of their 16 matches this year. The coach acknowledged that there is plenty of room for improvement but backed the young side to develop its aggressive style of cricket.“We don't pay too much attention to the form. You are talking about 16 T20Is in the last six months. But at the same time, we know what scope of improvement this team has got,” he said.“There is a huge scope of improvement. There is a young side. We are trying to play some good cricket, good aggressive cricket,'' he added.India will begin their Women's T20 Asia Cup campaign against Thailand on Sunday before turning their attention to the much-anticipated Pakistan clash on September 5.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: County Championship: Durham need four runs to beat Gloucestershire
articles.summary: Division Two leaders Durham will need four runs on the final day to beat Gloucestershire.
articles.body:
Rothesay County Championship, Division Two, Chester-le-Street (day three)

Gloucestershire 137: Aldridge 5-16 & 250: Hammond 58; Aldridge 4-47

Durham 384: Bedingham 122; Langridge 3-89

Durham (6 pts) need four runs to beat Gloucs (3 pts)

Bad light prevented Kasey Aldridge's superb nine-wicket match haul from delivering league leaders Durham a three-day County Championship win over bottom side Gloucestershire.

A devastating burst of 4-47 from the seam-bowling all-rounder backed up his first innings five-for, but the hosts' victory charge will roll into day four with only four to win as the weather meant their chase could not begin before close.

At the start of the day, Durham's tail boosted their first-innings total to 384 - a lead of 247 - thanks to cameos from Aldridge, Brydon Carse and Matthew Potts, before the latter pair reduced Gloucestershire to 7-2 second time around. They were later bowled out for 250.

Cameron Bancroft and Miles Hammond were able to guide the visitors to 50-2 at lunch.

A century stand for the fourth wicket halted Durham's progress before Aldridge produced a superb three-wicket spell on the brink of tea to reaffirm the home side's dominance in the match and the Division Two table.

Light dictated that Durham's Test-quality pace attack step aside with two wickets required, and an explosive 10th-wicket partnership of 39 between Sai Kishore (29 not out) and JT Langridge forced the league leaders to bat again.

With that target of four set, the players did not emerge from their dressing rooms, with Gloucestershire refusing to bowl spin, leaving as little as one ball of action in prospect for day four.

In the only fixture in the country to start on time, Durham resumed on 331-8 and swiftly accelerated beyond 350.

Carse took James Hayes for 16 in an over before he was bowled by the Nottinghamshire loanee for 20. Potts, who added 15, fell to Langridge, the seamer finishing with three wickets.

The England duo then produced a relentless opening burst which saw Gloucestershire stagger to 15-2 in 10 overs.

Joe Phillips was removed by Carse for the second time in the match for a duck, before Potts had Ollie Price caught behind. Bancroft and Hammond counter-attacked against the change bowlers to reach lunch with no further damage.

Both sides battled manfully after the break, with the left-handed Hammond negotiating a testing nine-over Ben Stokes spell to reach 50 off 80 balls.

He batted comfortably in partnership with captain Bancroft, but a rising delivery from Aldridge squared Hammond up and induced the edge for 58.

Aldridge continued his fine performance by having Bancroft caught at second slip for 46 in his next over, and new man Tommy Boorman followed shortly after.

Gloucestershire finished the session five down and still 115 in arrears, leaving five wickets left for Durham to complete the job.

As the gloom set in after tea, Aldridge uprooted Daz Ahmed's middle stump for a 14-ball duck to register nine wickets in a match for the first time in his career.

With a light reading taken, it seemed only the elements could save Gloucestershire, as first innings half-centurion James Bracey dug in alongside Mitch Killeen.

Carse removed Bracey with a vicious in-swinger - 173-7.

In the 61st over of the innings, light forced Colin Ackermann into the attack, and he struck with his second ball, ending a spirited hand from Killeen to leave his side two wickets away.

Ackermann bowled in partnership with Will Rhodes, while Kishore shone with two sixes in 29.

Ackermann accounted for Hayes, who chipped to mid-wicket and left his side nine down, still trailing by 36.

Kishore and Langdrige had fun against Durham's part-timers, eking out a slender lead with a succession of maximums which ended when Langridge holed out for 36.

Although the umpires returned to the middle, they soon trudged off, and play was called off just after 18:20 BST.

Durham are all but there for a seventh win in 10 games.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Michael Vaughan backs Dan Lawrence for run as all-rounder
articles.summary: Former captain Michael Vaughan backs batter Dan Lawrence for a run in England's Test side. How would you solve impending selection headache?
articles.body:
Former captain Michael Vaughan believes Dan Lawrence has shown enough to remain in the England Test side when Jacob Bethell returns from injury.

Lawrence, a batter who bowls part-time off-spin, was a surprise choice when he was picked to fill the role created by the retirement of all-rounder Ben Stokes earlier this summer.

But after making 51 in the first Test at Headingley, Lawrence impressed with 50 not out from 66 balls in tricky conditions on day three of the second Test against Pakistan.

"I think it is a really good selection," Vaughan told BBC Test Match Special. "He will have a period in the England side that we will enjoy watching him bat.

"I think in time his off-spin will come in very handy indeed."

Lawrence impresses as weather delays England

Lawrence hits half-century but rain disrupts England's progress again - as it happened

Lawrence, 29, was recalled after an international absence of almost two years, having averaged 26.84 across 14 previous Tests including a stint as a makeshift opener.

By picking him, England prioritised having four pace bowling options over a frontline spinner, with Lawrence backed to provided the overs of slow bowling if needed. He has only bowled one over in the series so far with pace bowlers dominant.

On Saturday Lawrence made his mark by coming to the crease at 83-4 and steering England to 177-7 in their second innings when rain brought an early close.

The right-hander, whose best Test score remains 91 , countered excessive seam movement and uneven bounce by showing attacking intent, hitting six fours and two sixes.

"He seems to read the game," Vaughan said. "It was the right way to play at that moment.

"He has a quirky technique that has worked for him and is very confident. He knows his scoring areas.

"He is clearly a better player than when he played for England last time."

England's current balance - with Lawrence picked over a frontline spinner - appears suited to home conditions, and could also work in South Africa and Australia where England play this winter.

While stronger spin options would likely be needed for the tour of Bangladesh in the new year, the success of England's pace quartet of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue has lessened the need for a spinner in home conditions and, in turn, helped Lawrence's cause.

Key selection decisions are still looming, however, with Jacob Bethell currently out of the series because of a knee injury.

Bethell, who also bowls part-time spin, could replace Lawrence, or regain his place from Jordan Cox, who has impressed with two fifties while filling in for Bethell at number three.

Other options include pushing Cox or Bethell up to open in place of Emilio Gay - Cox opened early in his career in county cricket and Bethell is England's current 50-over opener - and moving Cox down the order to replace Jamie Smith as wicketkeeper.

Smith scored an impressive 61 in England's first innings and has improved his glovework after a poor showing in the Ashes.

"It's pointless looking to the future because it hasn't happened yet," Lawrence said. "I'm just trying to contribute every Test I can and give a good showing of myself.

"Thankfully, so far, I think I have done.

"Obviously thoughts creep into your head and I'm desperate, along with all the other boys, to establish myself in an England shirt, which is something I haven't quite done in my career so far.

"It's just about trying to take every opportunity you get and really enjoy the occasion instead of feeling nervous about the occasion. Just have fun, play the cricket that's got me here this summer."

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Dan Lawrence's brilliant 50 lifts hosts to 357-run lead, as rain causes havoc on day three at Lord's
articles.summary: Rain delays caused havoc on day three of the second Test between England and Pakistan at Lord's as Dan Lawrence spurred the hosts on to a lead of 357 striking an impressive half-century; watch day four live on Sky Sports Cricket on Sunday from 10.15am
articles.body:
Lawrence battled hard to acclimatise to the uneven bounce on the Lord's pitch, but would surge to a superb 64-ball half-ton, which included a booming six to long-on, and lead England to a score of 177-7 at stumps.

Intermittent showers delayed proceedings for almost three-and-a-half hours on Saturday morning, with Emilio Gay and Harry Brook eventually taking to the field to bat at 2.20pm.

Mohammad Abbas took full advantage of the conditions, which were highly conducive to the pace bowlers, utilising the pitch's uneven bounce to jag the ball left and right and take impressive figures of 3-48.

Gay and Brook struggle in tricky conditions

Gay's time at the crease would be short-lived, with Abbas pinning the England opener lbw with an unplayable delivery in the second over of the day.

The England batter, who fought brilliantly on Friday evening, will feel hard done by the delivery after the ball skidded off the surface, bouncing low under his bat and onto his back pad.

After another rain delay, Brook (34), who had thought his way through his innings, edged Abbas behind to Mohammad Rizwan standing up to the crease.

It was another excellent piece of bowling from Abbas, who had played his four previous balls down the off side, before coming down much straighter to Brook, jagging the ball away to the off side.

With Rizwan up to the stumps, Brook couldn't get closer to the pitch of the ball and nullify its lateral movement, with the Yorkshireman ultimately edging behind.

While dark clouds loomed low over the Home of Cricket, the rain held off for another four overs before Abbas produced another jaffa to remove Jamie Smith (7).

This time, the ball nipped towards Smith's leg stump, and the wicketkeeper drove forward, pushing an inside edge to Shan Masood, who took the catch comfortably.

An early tea was called as rain began to fall again, but three balls after the break, Pakistan reduced England to 162-7, with Mohammad Ali forcing Gus Atkinson (7) to step across his crease before pinning him on the front pad.

Only 1.5 more overs were bowled before the heavens opened again and the grounds staff raced onto the pitch with the covers.

Fans waited for the players to return to the field and the sun finally broke through the gloom, but farcically, play was abandoned just after 6.30pm due to bad light.

Lawrence and Ollie Robinson (2no) will return to the crease on Sunday for day four.

Fans will be frustrated by bad light decision

Many fans had been left waiting in the stands at Lord's after the players were pulled off the field at 5.08pm due to rain.

The conditions gradually started to improve, but fears arose that both sides would not return to the pitch as the light began to fade.

Just after 6pm, grounds staff began to remove the covers and the sun broke through the clouds.

Both teams needed to be back on the field before 7pm for the match to continue through to the 7.30pm cut-off, and conditions had improved considerably by that point, to the extent that the game could have resumed.

However, the umpires, who have been commended for their efforts to keep play going throughout the opening two Tests, made the decision to abandon the match - a move that will understandably frustrate many of the fans inside the ground, who had already missed more than half a day of cricket due to the weather.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Nasser Hussain fumes as day three of second Test at Lord's abandoned during sunshine
articles.summary: Just 24.5 overs possible on Saturday of second Test due to bad light and rain; stumps called at 6.30pm despite sun shining; Dan Lawrence's sixth Test fifty, notched from 64 balls, features stunning six; watch day four from 10.15am, Sunday, Sky Sports Cricket
articles.body:
Just 24.5 overs were possible on a gloomy Saturday due to rain and bad light, during which time England moved from their overnight 81-3 to 177-7 for a lead of 357 as they look to wrap up a series win.

There looked to be a chance of more cricket when the sun began to shine late in the evening, only for the day to be officially called off just after 6.30pm local time, prompting heavy booing from spectators.

Had the players returned to the field before 7pm, play could have been extended to 7.30pm.

On hearing news of the abandonment, Sky Sports expert Hussain said: "That's a joke, honestly a joke. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is.

"These fans have waited here all afternoon for it to stop raining. It is now bright, blue sky in the distance. In about five minutes, it is going to be sunny here."

Speaking moments earlier, after noticing a lack of urgency to get the game on, Hussain said: "I have no idea what's going on and I don't think the fans do.

"It's the brightest it's been for about eight hours. It's not raining - get the covers off and start playing.

"This is the best conditions we have had and no one is doing anything."

'Eye-catching Lawrence got his tempo right'

In the small amount of cricket the fans did see, England's Dan Lawrence clinched a sixth Test half-century with his knock of 50 not out from 66 balls including a stunning six over extra-cover that Sky Sports pundit Dinesh Karthik called "the shot of the series".

Lawrence opted to counter-attack as Pakistan's bowlers found lavish movement and the pitch offered up uneven bounce - his England team-mate Emilio Gay was trapped lbw by Mohammad Abbad from an unplayable delivery that scuttled through low.

On Lawrence's innings, Hussain said: "He got his tempo right. This is not the surface to hang in on, there is a ball with your name on it - as Gay found out - so you have to score, put bowlers under pressure."

Hussain's fellow analyst Stuart Broad added: "Lawrence fought hard and played some eye-catching shots as well.

"He took his time to get in and get used to the pitch and then took it upon himself to put bowlers off their line and length, using his feet."

Lawrence: I'm just trying to contribute in every Test

Lawrence has replaced the retired Ben Stokes in England's XI, recalled after averaging 65.66 for Surrey in the County Championship this term and notching five hundreds.

His Lord's fifty against Pakistan followed a half-century in the series opener at Headingley.

Lawrence is also the chief spin bowling option at the moment as the side go in with an all-pace frontline attack of Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson.

The 29-year-old said: "I'm just trying to contribute every Test I can and give a good showing of myself. Thankfully, so far, I think I have done.

"I'm desperate, along with all the other boys, to establish myself in an England shirt, which is something I haven't quite done in my career so far.

"It's about trying to take every opportunity you get and really enjoy the occasion instead of feeling nervous. Have fun and play the cricket that's got me here this summer."

articles.title: England v Pakistan: Nasser Hussain calls early end to play at Lord's 'a joke'
articles.summary: The decision to abandon play an hour early after a rain-hit third day of England’s second Test against Pakistan is criticised by former captain Nasser Hussain and fans.
articles.body:
The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nasser Hussain.

On a Saturday badly affected by persistent showers at Lord's, players left the field at 17:08 BST.

At that point, prospects of conditions improving sufficiently for play to resume seemed remote. However, rain cleared and the sky brightened.

The groundstaff partially removed the covers while officials deliberated. At 18:30, with up to an hour of playing time remaining and with the weather the best it had been all day, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned proceedings.

The decision was greeted with booing by some of the sparse crowd that remained inside the ground.

"That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports.

"I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is.

"In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."

The weather stayed dry and the light remained good up to 19:30, the time at which play would have been scheduled to close.

The morning session had been washed out and only 24.5 overs of play were possible as the players dodged the showers, meaning spectators will receive a 50% refund on the price of their ticket.

If 30 overs had been completed, spectators would not have been entitled to any money back.

Still, the abandonment caused some fans to express their displeasure with messages to the BBC's live coverage of the Test.

"Sat in the Edrich Stand," wrote Joe at Lord's. "It hasn't rained for half an hour and it's as bright as it's been all day. Absolutely no justification for not playing right now. A real shame."

Rachel in Kingswinford added: "Ridiculous to call it off! They want fans supporting Test cricket and those spectators have stuck with it all day - another 30-45 mins of play would have been a better look (plus saving authorities money on refunds)!"

Another message from Paul in Northwich read: "This is a terrible advert for cricket. It's like the umpires are waiting for it to rain again. At least the spectators can get a refund."

Vaughan backs Lawrence for extended run in England team

Lawrence impresses as weather delays England

Play ended with England 177-7 in their second innings, 357 ahead and on course to win the match and series.

Batting conditions had been difficult all day and it would have been another challenging period for the home side had they been asked to return for a short time late in the evening.

"It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50.

"It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward.

"Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."

The situation at Lord's came on the same day Durham were denied the chance to chase a victory target of four against Gloucestershire because of bad light at the end of the third day of their County Championship match at Chester-le-Street.

It means the teams will return on Sunday for what could be as little as one ball of action.

Gloucestershire were dismissed for 250 in their second innings in the closing stages of Saturday, with visiting coach Mark Alleyne claiming the light was already too poor before his team were all out.

"I'm not sure where to start, really," said Alleyne. "I mean, 45 minutes before we lost the last wicket, it was too dark to play, which would have been consistent with all the other days that we played."

"We had probably 50 minutes of cricket there that we probably shouldn't have done."

The match could have been concluded had Gloucestershire chosen to bowl spin, only for the away side to refuse and push the game into a Sunday when rain is forecast.

"They asked if we would bowl our spinners to finish the game," added Alleyne. "Of course, we said no, we'll bowl our quick bowlers, in which case it became bad light, so we'll come back tomorrow."

Durham coach Ryan Campbell wrote on X: "Cricket sometimes doesn't help itself. Before everyone loads up on the poor old umpires, it's not their fault."

articles.title: Joe Root: What's behind the England captain's lbw struggles after twice more falling foul at Lord's
articles.summary: Joe Root has been dismissed lbw seven times across five Tests this summer, and nine times in his last 12 Test innings'; watch day four of the seond Test between England and Pakistan at Lord's, live on Sky Sports Cricket from 10.15am on Sunday (play starts 11am)
articles.body:
That was the debate during the rain-interrupted third day's play at Lord's, with the England captain twice succumbing leg before wicket during the second Test against Pakistan - taking his total to seven such dismissals this summer, and nine in his last 12 Test innings.

"It's fascinating that even a guy of more than 160 Tests, who averages over 50 - one of the greatest players England have ever produced - teams will still be looking at that developing trend," Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton said.

"It also reflects how the game is changing. When we started playing, many more bowlers were looking to take the ball away and challenge your outside edge.

"You were taught that Test cricket was played around off stump, or in the channel, and that the best bowlers get the ball to move away, with your danger area the slip cordon.

"What we've seen in recent times in England is bowlers moving to the wobble seam delivery much more, looking to nip the ball back.

"The number of lbws and bowled dismissals this summer is high, and that's how teams will be looking to have a crack at Root. They'll be trying to exploit that slight area of weakness.

"There's also the added context of the wicketkeeper coming up to the stumps to the slower, medium pace bowlers like Matt Henry and Mohammad Abbas - and that is what is keeping Root more in the crease.

"You have more chance of getting that lbw when the keeper is up."

Root's second-innings dismissal to Mohammad Ali came after the Pakistan pacer got one to nip and bounce away from the right-hander, beating the outside edge, the ball before.

Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain believes it's a contributing factor to Root's lbw struggles, with bowlers managing to set him up with the one that shapes away.

"The moment you see the ball moving away from you, you naturally go to cover the outside edge - Root will go across with that front pad," Hussain said.

"Because the ball is doing so much this summer, any batter will go slightly across with that front leg, as they are worried about the outside edge to the one moving away.

"But as Athers is talking about, the wobble seam then comes into it and nips back - you get four-and-a-quarter inches to cover a ball that's moving away and back in!

"It reminds me a little bit of Terry Alderman, who used to set Graham Gooch up like that: outswing, outswing, outswing, nip back. Goochy had to change his whole technique from back and across, to just back.

"If you watch Root at his best, he is a straight-line sort of batter, back and forward, he stays beside the ball.

"But because the ball is moving so much, he's trying to get across to it and that leaves him vulnerable to the lbw.

"Some of it is due to low bounce as well, especially on this ground [Lord's] - it brings the stumps and lbw into play.

"Bowlers are just holding a length, because they know they will find the stumps.

"And you have to also give the bowlers some credit. The skill we've seen from England, New Zealand, Pakistan this summer to bowl outswing and then wobble seam to bring in the lbw."

And that is Root's dilemma, Atherton added: "Nasser is right, because if Root said to himself, 'I'm going to take the lbw out of the equation and open up a bit', you then become more vulnerable to the outside edge.

"It's what makes this a fascinating game."
